title: epan: Store dependency graph adjacency list in set (hash table)
description:
The dependency graph (not actually used yet, see #1402) wants to
store each possible protocol adjacency only once. It's considerably
faster to store that in a set (GHashTable has facilities to work as
a set, saving space) than in a linked list where each item has to
be examined against all others (or else inserted sorted.)

Note that possibly these are stored in the wrong direction (one reason
why it took so long as a list is that all the BT ATT dissectors are
registered as adjacent in the list of their parent protocol.)

notes.body:
added 15 commits
  • 70d257c6...bb83e004 - 14 commits from branch wireshark:master
  • 5bd86528 - epan: Store dependency graph adjacency list in set (hash table)
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/20526/diffs?diff_id=1421859896&start_sha=70d257c6ee002bf3c139c18ac27ee2848b1bf1ef)
I agree with the hash table being faster, but I believe the list was chosen for more efficient iteration when walking the list of dependencies (that functionality has yet to be done)

Iterating over the hash table should still be O(N) with a GHashTableIter; it's not as efficient as using the hash table in other ways, but it's not particularly worse than a list. It's worse if you need to walk in a particular order, but would that actually be necessary?

It's also considerably faster if you switch which protocol is the parent of the list, mostly because hundreds of Bluetooth Attribute dissectors are added to the same list, whereas if they each had a list it wouldn't be so bad. It's mostly the checking to see if something has already been added to the list that makes it slow.

Or alternatively, it would be faster if the integer proto ids were used instead of the strings as the hashing would be faster.

This is roughly 5% of the startup time for TShark. There are a few other big things out there (the XML dissector reading DTDs for registering protocols using flex, checking to see if protocol names use valid characters and don't have a doubled ".." - that last part considerably slows things down), but this has a surprisingly large impact.
